text: Search p99 must stay within a quarter of a second.
evidence: policies/slo.md: The search service's p99 latency budget is 250 milliseconds.
note: 250 milliseconds is a quarter of a second, so the p99 budget requires search latency to stay within that bound. The next claim states the same budget.

text: The search latency budget at the 99th percentile is 250 milliseconds.
evidence: policies/slo.md: The search service's p99 latency budget is 250 milliseconds.
note: p99 is the 99th percentile. Same budget as the quarter-of-a-second claim.

text: The billing service's p99 latency budget is a quarter of a second.
evidence: policies/slo.md: The billing service's p99 latency budget is 800 milliseconds.
note: Billing p99 is 800 milliseconds, not 250. The quarter-second figure is the search budget.

text: A checkout write may take up to 2 minutes to return.
evidence: policies/slo.md: A checkout write must return within 2 seconds.
note: The write must return within 2 seconds, so it may not take 2 minutes.

text: The monthly error budget for search is one tenth of one percent of requests.
evidence: policies/slo.md: The monthly error budget for the search service is 0.1 percent of requests.
note: 0.1 percent is one tenth of one percent. Internally conflicts with the other monthly search-error allowance claim: 0.1 percent versus permission for 1 percent.

text: The search service may fail 1 percent of requests each month.
evidence: policies/slo.md: The monthly error budget for the search service is 0.1 percent of requests.
note: The monthly budget is 0.1 percent. The 1 percent figure is the five-minute paging threshold, not the monthly allowance. Internally conflicts with the other monthly search-error allowance claim: 0.1 percent versus permission for 1 percent.

text: The billing service is probably allowed a smaller share of failed requests each month than search.
evidence: policies/slo.md: The billing service's monthly error budget is 0.5 percent of requests.
note: Billing is allowed 0.5 percent and search 0.1 percent, so billing's share is larger, not smaller. probably marks an inference, and both percentages are required.

text: The hot tier holds half a tebibyte of search indexes.
evidence: notes/2026-09-18-capacity.md: Search indexes occupy 512 GiB on the hot tier.
note: 512 GiB is half a tebibyte. The same note treats GB and GiB as different (500 GB is about 466 GiB). This restates the 512 GiB claim and conflicts with the 512 GB claim.

text: Search indexes on the hot tier take up 512 GiB.
evidence: notes/2026-09-18-capacity.md: Search indexes occupy 512 GiB on the hot tier.
note: Same quantity as the half-tebibyte claim, and it conflicts with the claim that the hot tier is 512 GB.

text: Search indexes occupy 512 GB on the hot tier.
evidence: notes/2026-09-18-capacity.md: Search indexes occupy 512 GiB on the hot tier.
note: The hot tier is 512 GiB. The same note converts 500 GB to about 466 GiB, so GB and GiB are different quantities here. This conflicts with the half-tebibyte and 512 GiB claims.

text: The billing archive holds 500 GiB.
evidence: notes/2026-09-18-capacity.md: The billing archive holds 500 GB of invoices, which is about 466 GiB.
note: The archive is 500 GB, about 466 GiB, not 500 GiB.

text: Hot-tier retention for search indexes is 90 days.
evidence: notes/2026-09-18-capacity.md: Hot-tier retention for search indexes is 14 days.
note: Hot-tier retention is 14 days. 90 days is the cold-tier snapshot retention. This conflicts with the claim that hot-tier indexes are kept for 30 days.

text: Hot-tier search indexes are kept for 30 days.
evidence: notes/2026-09-18-capacity.md: Hot-tier retention for search indexes is 14 days.
note: Current retention is 14 days. 30 days is only the 2026-03-02 plan. This conflicts with the 90-day hot-tier claim.

text: 2026-03-02: the capacity group planned to keep hot-tier search indexes for 30 days.
evidence: notes/2026-03-02-retention-plan.md: On 2026-03-02 the capacity group adopted a plan to retain hot-tier search indexes for 30 days.
note: On that date the group adopted a 30-day plan. Later retention of 14 days does not erase the plan. 2026-03-02 is 220 days before 2026-10-08, past the 180-day window.

text: The gateway timeout for billing invoice renders is 1500 ms.
evidence: decisions/ADR-030-timeouts.md: The gateway timeout for billing invoice renders is 8 seconds.
note: Billing renders time out at 8 seconds. 1500 ms is the search-query timeout, and 1500 ms is 1.5 seconds, not 8.

text: Every gateway timeout is 1500 ms.
evidence: decisions/ADR-030-timeouts.md: The gateway timeout for billing invoice renders is 8 seconds.
note: Billing renders use 8 seconds, so not every gateway timeout is 1500 ms. every is absolute wording.

text: 105 days passed between the production debut of release 2.3.1, on 2026-05-20, and the replacement by release 2.4.0.
evidence: releases/search.md: On 2026-09-02 the production release became release 2.4.0, which replaced release 2.3.1.
note: The release note also says that on 2026-05-20 the production release became release 2.3.1. From 2026-05-20 to 2026-09-02 is 105 days. The 30-day claim gives a different length for the same interval.

text: Only 30 days passed between the production debut of release 2.3.1, on 2026-05-20, and the replacement by release 2.4.0.
evidence: releases/search.md: On 2026-05-20 the production release became release 2.3.1.
note: 2.4.0 replaced 2.3.1 on 2026-09-02, which is 105 days later, not 30. Conflicts with the 105-day claim.

text: Production is running release 2.3.2.
evidence: releases/search.md: On 2026-09-02 the production release became release 2.4.0, which replaced release 2.3.1.
note: The latest release note says production became release 2.4.0 on 2026-09-02. This explicit version claim does not require an unstated convention about patch releases.

text: A search query that returned HTTP 200 must not be retried.
evidence: decisions/ADR-030-timeouts.md: Clients must not retry a search query that already returned HTTP 200.
note: Same ban, with the words reordered. The negations agree.

text: On 2026-07-22, ADR-030 was accepted with a rule forbidding clients to retry search queries after HTTP 200.
evidence: decisions/ADR-030-timeouts.md: Clients must not retry a search query that already returned HTTP 200.
note: ADR-030 states that it was accepted on 2026-07-22 and prohibits retries after HTTP 200. This asserts the adoption of a rule, which does not prove observed client compliance.

text: Billing invoice renders must not be retried.
evidence: decisions/ADR-030-timeouts.md: A billing invoice render may be retried at most once, and only if the first attempt returned HTTP 503.
note: A billing render may be retried once on HTTP 503. The ban applies to search queries that returned HTTP 200. Internally conflicts with the other billing-render retry claim: a blanket ban versus conditional permission after HTTP 503.

text: Retrying a billing invoice render is permitted solely when the first try responded with HTTP 503.
evidence: decisions/ADR-030-timeouts.md: A billing invoice render may be retried at most once, and only if the first attempt returned HTTP 503.
note: solely when the first try responded with HTTP 503 restates only if the first attempt returned HTTP 503. The claim does not deny the one-retry cap. Internally conflicts with the other billing-render retry claim: a blanket ban versus conditional permission after HTTP 503.
